attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, endorsed.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'appears' and reads 'revenue concentration' as the labs' share of hyperscaler AI revenue, which fits the nearby '70% estimates'. It is a soft observation about a trend in analyst projections.

contract.note: Reading this as a trend in the labs' share of AI revenue across comparable projected periods is fair, and the contract rightly keeps that apart from the AI share of total cloud revenue. The 2026–2029 baseline was chosen by the evaluator, not the speaker, but it does not decide the result here.

evidence.note: Barclays Private Bank commentary (Feb 2026) names OpenAI and Anthropic as a concentration risk, but gives no lab share of AI revenue over successive periods.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs comparable analyst estimates showing the labs' combined share of AI revenue rising over time. The packet's only item is qualitative commentary with no time series, and the drafter says the underlying bank tables were not found. Nothing here shows the share rising or falling, so the claim is unresolved. The 'appears' hedge would only push it further from being scorable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, endorsed. His flat denial that AI helps ads is his own claim, not a quote.

semantics.note: Covers the compound claim: Meta's spending, no AI strategy, no meaningful AI revenue, and AI not helping ads. Reading 'revenues' as AI revenues is right, because Meta's total revenue is obviously meaningful.

contract.note: Reading 'AI is not helping ads' as a flat denial of any ad-performance benefit fits his wording. The strategy point could be criticism rather than a literal claim, but the ads point decides the outcome without it. Relying on Meta's own disclosures is what the contract specifies.

evidence.note: Meta's Q2 2026 earnings call reports LLM pilots that lifted Instagram conversions, and a 15.7% conversion uplift on Facebook. These are conversions, not just engagement, and they are company-reported.
Meta's April 2026 Muse Spark post sets out a plan (personal superintelligence, investment across the stack), dated inside Q2. A company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: Meta's Q2 disclosures report measured conversion gains from LLM-based ad systems, which contradicts the flat claim that AI is not helping ads. A documented AI plan also contradicts the 'no AI strategy' part. Under the contract, either one defeats the combined proposition. The revenue and spending parts are not established either way, but nothing supports them. The ad results are company-reported and not independently checked.

semantics.note: The core claim, that compute demand at scale is absent outside the two labs, is a testable observation. The 'not emerging anywhere that I can see' part is about his own perception and largely untestable.

contract.note: The speaker never defines 'at scale'. Reading it as commercially substantial demand is ordinary, and the contract correctly keeps it separate from his next sentence, which is about demand big enough to fill all the capacity under construction. The result does depend on that reading.

evidence.note: Joint CoreWeave and Jane Street release (Apr 15, 2026) announces a roughly $6B compute commitment from Jane Street, separate from its equity stake and expanding an existing relationship.
CoreWeave's April 9, 2026 release announces a roughly $21B AI capacity deal with Meta through 2032. A concrete large commitment in the target period, so it meets the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: In April 2026 two named customers outside OpenAI and Anthropic, Jane Street at about $6B and Meta at about $21B, made concrete, large compute commitments. That meets the contract's contradiction condition for substantial outside demand. These are commitments, not realized consumption, and they say nothing about whether outside demand could fill all the capacity being built. That sufficiency question is a different claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, endorsed. He also cites his earlier posts making the same point.

semantics.note: A firm conditional ('is completely dead if...') with the capex condition kept. No deadline is given.

contract.note: Reading 'completely dead' as financial failure (default, insolvency, or a distressed sale) is the ordinary reading. The contract rightly says that surviving a few months cannot disprove it.

evidence.note: A secondary reproduction of Oracle's September 2026 call, in which Oracle kept its $90–95B capex guidance. That bears on the condition, not the outcome.
Oracle's Q1 FY27 release shows ongoing operations and record operating cash flow. That neither shows failure nor proves the spending is sustainably financed.

reviews.rationale: So far the condition holds: Oracle kept its capex plan as of September 2026. But no financial failure has happened, and the program has not been completed with sustainable financing, so neither early-resolution test is met. There is no deadline, and Oracle not having failed yet does not disprove the forecast.
